items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: when Kenny Clarke and Monk and Dizzy and all those people made that music at Minton’s

ctx.x: Was it out of the ordinary for this — this was an integrated group at the time — was it out of the ordinary?

Yes, but not as much as it is now in a way. I mean curiously now — this should be another discussion. I didn’t feel any problem. I have felt the problem at various times but not this time. I don’t know why. It would be interesting to go into that. But later, you know bebop had a social agenda as you probably know, when I say bebop I mean that’s not a secret — I don’t know if they did it consciously or not — but when Kenny Clarke and Monk and Dizzy and all those people made that music at Minton’s, part of the…

is these guys are gifted they’re geniuses, but somehow or other it’s also natural and they’re different. They don’t need to be educated and they just came full blown from the head of Zeus — and French people particularly had that kind of attitude. And that ain’t the way it is, or was. And the facts are that the society at the time said white or black, if you wanted to make a living playing this kind of music you must entertain with it. You can’t just stand up there and play music to listen to. That’s not what…
